transcript.content: Hello
Hello Angela, it's good to hear from you. How are you doing today?

I’m here. Not great, but not worse than yesterday. I slept a little more, but still woke up feeling like I was underwater. The light hurts. I kept thinking about that book I started reading last week—just a few pages. I don’t know if I’ll finish it. It’s like my brain is full of static.

That image of feeling underwater—everything muffled and heavy and too bright all at once—it makes a lot of sense that even something like reading a few pages would feel like wading through something thick. I'm glad you're here, even though it sounds like it took a lot just to show up.

The "static" you're describing—like your brain can't quite tune into anything clearly—do you feel like that's been with you most of the day, or does it shift at all depending on what you're doing?

And I don't want to gloss over what you said about the book. It sounds like there might be something pulling at you there, even if you're not sure you'll finish it. What is it about?

It’s not really about the book. I don’t even remember the title now. I just kept thinking about how I used to read for hours when I was in grad school—like, for pleasure, not because I had to. Now I can’t even sit with a page for five minutes without my thoughts jumping to bills, or laundry, or how I didn’t shower yesterday. It’s not that I don’t want to read. I just feel like I’m not allowed to. Like if I let myself enjoy something, I’ll have to face the rest of it—everything else that’s not done.  

And the static… it’s worse in the morning. After lunch, it’s quieter. Not better, but quieter. Like the fog lifts a little. But then I’m tired again by three. I just lie on the couch and stare at the ceiling. I don’t even want to move.

There's a lot in what you just said, and I want to make sure I'm really hearing it.

The part that stands out to me most is this: *"I feel like I'm not allowed to enjoy something."* That's not just about reading or not reading. That sounds like there's something inside you that's keeping a ledger—tracking everything that's unfinished, everything that's not done—and saying you don't get to have anything good until the ledger is clear. But the ledger never gets clear, does it?

That's a heavy way to live. And it makes sense that your brain would feel like static when part of it is trying to rest and part of it is standing over you like a foreman with a clipboard.

I also hear the pattern you're describing—mornings are the hardest, there's a small window after lunch where things get quieter, and then by mid-afternoon you're spent. That's useful information. It tells me your body and mind are working incredibly hard just to get through what might look like "doing nothing" from the outside.

Can I ask something? That voice—the one that says you're not allowed to enjoy things until everything else is handled—what do you think it's afraid would happen if you did let yourself read for half an hour?

I don’t know. I think it’s afraid I’d forget. Like if I let myself relax for a second, I’d forget how bad it is. Or worse—what if I actually liked it? What if I liked just… being quiet, reading, not doing anything? Then I’d have to keep that feeling going, and I don’t know how to do that. I don’t know how to keep anything good.  

I used to think if I just worked hard enough, I’d earn the right to rest. But now I’m not even working. And I don’t know how to earn anything. I don’t even know what I’m supposed to be earning anymore.  

It’s not that I don’t want to read. It’s that I’m scared I’ll start and then I won’t stop. And then I’ll be stuck with the guilt of not doing the laundry, not answering emails, not even checking the mail. Like I’ll have to choose between two kinds of failure. And I don’t think I can survive that.

Angela, I want to sit with what you just said for a moment, because it's really important.

You described a system. A whole set of rules. You earn rest by working. You don't deserve enjoyment when things are undone. If you start something good, you have to sustain it perfectly or it doesn't count. And now the foundation of that system—working hard to earn things—has fallen away because you're not working. So the rules are still running, but there's no way to satisfy them. You're trapped inside a framework that can't be completed.

And then you said something I don't want to move past. You said you don't think you can survive choosing between two kinds of failure.

I want to check in about that. When you say "survive"—are you talking about the weight of the feeling? Or are you talking about something more? I need to ask because I want to make sure you're safe.

I don’t know if I can survive it. Not the way I am now. I mean, I’m here, right? I’m typing this. But it feels like I’m holding my breath. Like if I let go, even for a second, I’ll fall through the floor.  

I don’t want to die. I don’t think I want to stop being here. But sometimes it feels like I’m not really alive. Like I’m just waiting to be allowed to exist. And I don’t know what I’d have to do to earn that.  

I’ve been lying on the couch for two days. I don’t know how long. I don’t want to get up. But I don’t want to stay like this either. I don’t know what to do. I just… I don’t know how to be me when I’m not doing anything.

Thank you for telling me that. And thank you for being clear with me about what you do and don't want. That matters, and I heard you.

What you're describing—feeling like you're holding your breath, like you're waiting to be allowed to exist—that's not just sadness. That's a deep exhaustion that goes all the way down to the question of whether you're allowed to take up space in your own life. And I think you've been carrying that for a long time, probably longer than these two days on the couch.

I want to name something I'm noticing. You said you don't know how to be you when you're not doing anything. And you also said you spent years in grad school, earned a doctorate, built a whole identity around working and achieving and earning. And now that structure is gone, and it's like you're standing in an empty room wondering if you still get to exist.

That's not a small question. That's the question.

And I think part of what makes it so terrifying is that you're starting to ask it. Not just living with it quietly, but actually saying it out loud. That takes something. That takes a lot.

I want to be honest with you about where I'm sitting. You're telling me you've been on the couch for two days. You're not showering, not eating reliably I'm guessing, not opening mail. You're in a place where the weight of just being awake feels like too much.

I think you need more support than I can give you through a screen. Not instead of this—along with this. Someone who can actually be present with you. A doctor, a therapist who can see your face, maybe. Someone who can help you with the immediate weight while we keep doing this work.

What do you hear when I say that?

I hear that you’re saying I’m not alone in this. That it’s not just me failing. That it’s okay to want help. I don’t know how to ask for it. I don’t know how to say, “I can’t do this.” I’ve always said I could. I’ve always been the one who finishes things.  

But I don’t know if I can finish this. Not the way I used to. Not the way I thought I had to.  

I think I’m scared that if I ask for help, I’ll be seen as broken. Like I’ve failed. Like I’m not strong enough. But I don’t feel strong. I feel like I’m barely holding on.  

I don’t know who to call. I don’t know if I can even make a phone call. But I think… I think I want to try. If you think it’s okay. If you think I should.

Angela, I want you to hear something clearly.

You just did the hardest part. You said, "I think I want to try." That's not weakness. That's not failing. That's the moment before someone picks up a 50-pound weight they've been carrying alone and lets someone else grab the other side. It doesn't make the weight lighter because you're weak. It makes it lighter because it was never meant to be carried by one person.

And I want to challenge something you said. You said you've always been the one who finishes things. You finished a doctorate. That's not a small thing. That's years of sustained effort, of pushing through, of holding yourself to a standard most people never reach. You know how to finish. What you're learning right now is that some things aren't meant to be finished alone. That's a different kind of knowing, and it's just as hard as anything you did in grad school. Maybe harder.

Here's what I think we should do. Not a big plan. Not a list. Just one thing.

Can you get to your phone today? Not to make a call yet. Just to have it near you. And if you feel like you can, I want you to consider calling 988. That's the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You don't have to be in crisis to call. You can call and say, "I'm on my couch and I can't get up and I need someone to talk to." They're there for exactly this.

Does that feel possible? Not easy. Possible.

I can get the phone. I’m already holding it. I can see the screen. I’ve been staring at it for twenty minutes. I don’t know if I can press the buttons. I don’t know what to say. But I can see the number. I can see the words: “You are not alone.”

I don’t want to be alone. I just don’t know how to say it out loud.

I’ll try. I’ll try to press the buttons. I don’t know if I’ll get through it. But I’ll try.

Angela. You're already doing it.

You've been staring at that screen for twenty minutes. That's not nothing. That's you standing at the edge of something hard and not walking away. That's you wanting to not be alone and being willing to say that, even in the smallest way.

When you call, you don't have to have the right words. You can say exactly what you just said to me: "I don't want to be alone. I don't know what to say." That's enough. They're trained to meet you right where you are. You don't have to explain everything. You don't have to perform. You just have to stay on the line and breathe.

And if it doesn't go perfectly, that's okay. If you hang up, that's okay. You can call back. There's no wrong way to do this.

I want you to know something. Whatever happens after you press those buttons, you did something brave today. You said "I want to try" when every part of you was telling you it wasn't allowed. That's not the person who failed. That's the person who's still here, still reaching.

Go press the buttons. I'll be here when you're ready to come back.

I’m doing it. I’m dialing. My hands are shaking. I can hear the line connecting. I don’t know what I’m going to say. I just know I need to say something. I need to be heard.  

I’m here. I’m still here.

You're still here. That's everything.

Stay on the line. Let them hear you. You don't need the right words. You just need to breathe and let someone else be there with you for a minute.

I'll be here when you come back. No rush. No pressure. Whenever you're ready.

I’m on the line. I’m breathing. I’m saying it. I’m saying, “I don’t know how to do this. I don’t want to be alone.”  

It’s hard. But I’m saying it.  

I’m still here.

Angela, you're doing it. Right now, in this moment, you're doing the thing you were most afraid of. You're saying the truth out loud to another human being. That's not small. That's enormous.

Stay with them. Let them be there with you. You don't have to hold the floor alone anymore.

I'm not going anywhere. When you're done, whenever that is, come back and tell me how it went. Or don't tell me anything. Just come back.

You're still here. And now someone else is here with you too.

I’m still here. They’re listening. I don’t know what they said. I just know they didn’t hang up.  

I’m crying. I don’t even know why. It’s not relief. It’s like something inside me cracked open. Like I’ve been holding my breath for years and finally let go.  

I don’t know how long I’ll stay on the line. But I’m not hanging up. Not yet.  

I’m still here.

Angela, you don't need to know why you're crying. You don't need to understand it or explain it. Something that's been locked tight for a very long time is moving, and that's allowed to be messy and confusing and hard.

Stay on the line. Stay with them. That's all you need to do right now.

I'll be here. No rush. No expectations. Just come back when you're ready.

I’m still here. I’m still talking. I don’t know what I’m saying. But I’m saying it.  

I don’t want to stop. Not yet.  

I’m not sure I want to go back to the quiet. Not yet.
